sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E3879. The transcript contains transcription errors, incomplete phrases, and several events containing speaker changes; these are preserved in quotations and marked U where inseparable. Attribution follows turn context rather than ideology. No identifiable edited teaser replays occur in the supplied text. Historical quotations and empirical claims were not independently verified.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: to the untrained mind of course the defibrillator may sound absurd
candidates.explanation: Wood anticipates rejection by describing an untrained mind and inherited blind faith (E81–89), potentially discounting objections through a critic's defect. However, he then supplies an extended argument beginning E92. The text does not establish that every substantive objection is dismissed this way; this is possible protection, not a confirmed unsupported slogan.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: whether it's confirmed or disconfirmed is confirmation of the scientific hypothesis
candidates.explanation: Both outcomes of every scientific test are explicitly counted as confirmation, then linked to theism (E497–545). This protects that claimed evidential relationship against contrary experimental results. Wood supplies historical and conceptual reasons, so this remains an argument rather than slogan substitution; successful testing can reasonably support intelligibility without independently establishing its theological explanation.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: some of us just go one god further
candidates.explanation: The phrase moves from shared rejection of many gods toward rejecting the remaining god, without showing that the evidential cases are equivalent. Its role is ambiguous: E615 explicitly introduces a thought experiment, and E638–649 separately makes the narrower, defensible point that generic theism does not establish Yahweh. No objection-neutralizing device appears.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: once you step outside of that where you have no moral standard that you could possibly defend
candidates.explanation: Wood disqualifies the atheist's suffering objection through the alleged impossibility of defending its moral standard (E1445–1475), insulating theism from that external criticism. He offers an ordinary grounding argument, not a replacement catchphrase. Fairly, E1467–1469 explicitly permits Christians to discuss evil; the exclusion concerns external critics rather than all criticism.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: those gaps will be filled ultimately this is what we do
candidates.explanation: The assurance may replace justification for eventual resolution of the particular cosmological gaps under discussion. However, Shermer supplies historical examples earlier (E743–798) and explicitly calls current proposals unconfirmed at E1656–1660. The phrase may be optimistic extrapolation rather than evidential substitution; it does not itself stipulate that contrary results must confirm naturalism.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: they're heretical rebellious christians because they've adopted a christian worldview and just don't know it
candidates.explanation: Wood reclassifies atheists who practice science as unwitting Christians, neutralizing their apparent counterexample to Christian exclusivity. His historical argument supplies a proposed origin for scientific assumptions (E1855–1878), but does not establish that accepting those assumptions constitutes Christianity or rebellion. The identity declaration performs that missing inferential step.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: no amount of science is ever going to disconfirm their views it'll only add more confirmation
candidates.explanation: After Shermer's intervening reply, Wood explicitly renews the claim that every test outcome confirms the initial framework and its underlying beliefs (E1973–1993). The categorical statement protects those views from scientific disconfirmation. It summarizes his already supplied dependency argument, however disputed, so protection does not make it an unsupported slogan.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: there's just the normal the natural and the stuff we haven't explained yet
candidates.explanation: The formula excludes supernatural classification regardless of discovery: E2280–2286 says anything found becomes natural, otherwise nothing requires explanation. This protects the classification, although Shermer allows unfamiliar phenomena to exist in E2248–2279. Historical debunkings supply reasons for caution, leaving uncertain whether the universal affirmation substitutes for justification or merely defines his terminology.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: if i can't understand the problem without theism i i just can't i can't see this being a problem
candidates.explanation: Asked directly about dying children, Wood again makes the objection depend on theism and declines its force against belief (E2511–2531). This protects against that criticism through a claimed prerequisite, rather than answering the suffering itself. He supplies moral-grounding reasons and permits theistic wrestling with evil, making this a protected argument rather than slogan substitution.

candidates.speaker: O
candidates.quote: they will have an eternal life of forever lasting peace and is that not greater
candidates.explanation: The audience questioner expressly answers the suffering objection with guaranteed, greater eternal compensation (E3443–3454), making children's deaths compatible with crediting God regardless of the earthly loss. This is an unsupported compensatory argument rather than a compact slogan. Wood later limits his own treatment to possible coherence, expressly withholding a truth claim (E3505–3532).

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: when someone says hey i was sick and i got better i generally think now you just got better
contrasts.explanation: Wood accepts ordinary recovery as an alternative explanation, distinguishes personal belief from certainty, and makes a resurrection claim depend on a further debate about whether it happened. This qualifies miracle inference rather than guaranteeing divine confirmation.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: because you love your wife and you don't want to hurt her
contrasts.explanation: Shermer supplies concrete reasons for fidelity: care, promises, reciprocity, and the consequences of widespread dishonesty. He expressly identifies suffering as his moral starting point. That leaves the ultimate grounding dispute open, but the passage offers reasons rather than substituting an affirmation for them.
